blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

We see that a UVC was put into [Baby A] under sterile conditions, but it wasn't ideally placed, it was removed, another attempt was made, but again that had to be removed as well, and therefore the decision was taken, rather than having a UVC or a UAC, [Baby A] would be given a long line.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Thank you. If we move on now, please, Mr Murphy, to tile 154, we will come to Dr Harkness' insertion of a long line, one of, the jury will remember, three he was doing in room 1 that evening.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You have recorded this event, professor, at your paragraph 3.19; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it is, yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Thank you. The next matter that you record in your statement or your report is at paragraph 3.20 where you refer to nursing notes made for the night shift; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: For the jury's information, we see those at tile 170, please. There is a summary there, but essentially you refer to these as having been written the following morning at 07.58 in the morning; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: That the observations at 8 pm were stable?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And that glucose infusions had commenced via the long line as directed by Dr Harkness?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: You also refer in the subsequent paragraph to other matters recorded in the nursing notes, namely that [Baby A] was noted to be "jittery"; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Then at 20.20, that the person you describe as the nurse looking after [Baby A], who we know to be Lucy Letby, noticed that his hands were white, he was centrally pale with poor perfusion and had become apnoeic.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: You then record the fact that Dr Harkness was called to assist, that the glucose infusion was disconnected, that [Baby A] then collapsed, and you record the fact that his death was recorded as having occurred at 20.58 that evening.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do you then refer to what the jury has at tile 183?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If Mr Murphy would just find that for us, please. These are Dr Harkness' retrospective notes recording the fact that he was called to see [Baby A] at 20.26.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: That respiratory support had been given to him and that there was good chest movement. If we just -- I'm not going to do this very often with you, Professor Kinsey, but it's really for the benefit of the rest of us who need to remind ourselves of the factual circumstances.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So if we could go to the underlying material, please, Mr Murphy, at 1065.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There we see the fact recorded by Dr Harkness that respiratory support with bagging had started via Neopuff immediately and that there was good chest movement from [Baby A].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: You refer to evidence that we heard that Dr Harkness had got the impression that there might have been an issue relating to the long line which was removed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: That [Baby A] was intubated at 20.28?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: His heart rate was between 60 and 70 beats a minute?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And that chest compressions then started at 20.28 and he was given a saline bolus and a bolus of adrenaline at 20.31 and 20.33 respectively?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: You at your paragraph 3.29 record that Dr Jayaram then arrived.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, the consultant on call. I didn't know it was Dr Jayaram.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: I don't think you knew his identity. I'm inserting the names for my own and the jury's benefit, really.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So Dr Jayaram arrived, the UVC was pulled back, there was no heart rate detected, there was pulseless electrical activity on the monitor, and there then followed full CPR with multiple doses of adrenaline, sodium bicarbonate and dextrose.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And those efforts, unhappily, had to be discontinued at 20.58?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: At your paragraph 3.30, you then record what Dr Jayaram spoke of in a witness statement concerning an unusual skin discolouration that he had observed on [Baby A] at around this time.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: What you record him having recorded as being "flitting patches of pink areas on the background of a blue-y/grey skin, which appeared and disappeared"?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And which he said didn't fit with anything he had seen before?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Finally, so far as the background was concerned, at your paragraph 3.31, did you record the fact of a post-mortem
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: examination conducted by Dr Shukla of Alder Hey Hospital in Liverpool?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: The fact that no cause of death could be determined?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So I understand, yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: You record an anatomical variation of [Baby A]'s pulmonary arteries, which was thought unlikely to be significant?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And you also record something called a patent foramen ovale. Have I pronounced it right, first of all?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, you have and yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Can you explain to the jury what that is, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I can. I expect we may be coming on to this later because I have provided some diagrams for further discussion. In babies, before they are born, there is a bypass of the lungs' blood circulation, so the pulmonary circulation. And this circulation goes from the right side of the heart to the left side of the heart. Normally, when people are born, so in all of us sitting in this room now, the right side of the heart sends blood into the lungs for oxygenation and that comes back to the left side of the heart, once it's oxygenated, and the blood continues round the body to provide oxygen to all the organs to keep us going.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Because, when in the womb, a baby doesn't have use of their lungs, because they're swimming around in a pool of amniotic fluid, the placenta takes over the job of the lungs for oxygenation of the baby's blood supply, so the blood doesn't need to go through the lungs, apart from a tiny amount helping the lungs to grow.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So there's a bypass mechanism between the right atrium, which is the first chamber of the chart on the right-hand side of circulation, through to the left atrium, which is the first chamber on the left-hand side of the heart. That hole is the -oh dear, foramen ovale. Foramen is a window and ovale is oval, so it's an oval window, which is really a flap. It's a bit of membrane that is pushed against by the greater side pressure levels so that in a preterm -- well, in a baby in utero, the circulation goes through the patent foramen ovale omitting to go through the lungs. This is normal.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Have I explained this sufficiently?
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So the foramen ovale is between the right and left parts of the circulation, is normal in preterm babies and neonates, and it closes in most people.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Thank you. That will become relevant at a later stage and we'll run through the diagram and your explanation as to how this mechanism works, how it changes between a baby that's in its mother's womb and a baby after birth.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Okay. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm going to move on now, please, professor, to your section 4 of your report. Within the medical records relating to [Baby A], did you find the results of a full blood count test taken that had been undertaken on 6 July at just after 10 pm?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Just to put that into context for the jury, that's about an hour and three quarters after he had been born?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Others can ask you if it's thought to be necessary, but putting it in a sentence, was [Baby A]'s full blood count normal or abnormal?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It was normal of a child of his gestational age, yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Thank you. The jury will recall from the evidence that a cause for concern in relation to both [Baby A] and [Baby B] was the maternal antiphospholipid syndrome from which [Mother of Babies A & B] suffered.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Could we start, please, with you explaining to us what antiphospholipid syndrome is?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. So antiphospholipid syndrome is a rare autoimmune disease which affects the general systemic situation in the mother and causes antibodies. This is a rare disease in approximately 50 per 100,000 people.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: It often occurs in cases of other autoimmune disorders, but most commonly something called SLE, which is an abbreviation of systemic lupus erythematosus; again, a rare autoimmune condition.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: The problem with people with antiphospholipid syndrome is they make antibodies against their own tissues and so these tissues tend to start to work badly or not normally and can be associated with increased blood clotting. As a result, part of the management is to be on anti-coagulation with drugs such as warfarin and with heparin and also aspirin.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: It is well recognised in antiphospholipid syndrome that women who are pregnant can have problems both themselves during pregnancy and also that the unborn child may also have issues because of poor development of the placenta on the maternal side, and quite often mothers end up with very high blood pressure, which is hypertension, and is called pre-eclampsia in pregnancy.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: This is because the antibodies in antiphospholipid syndrome target the placental tissues in particular.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Because of problems with the placenta it means that the baby or babies that are trying to grow in the womb don't get the same amount of nutrients and blood flow and oxygenation as one would hope to see and therefore this can cause foetal growth retardation and potential issues for the unborn child.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Quite a lot of pregnancies in women with APS tend to have to have intervention with caesarean section of young babies in order to save the mother's life as well as that of the unborn children.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So would it be an oversimplification to say that antiphospholipid syndrome is likely to result in premature birth?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Results in clotting problems for the mother?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And therefore can endanger both mother and baby?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: As a result of problems with the placenta, yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Is antiphospholipid syndrome hereditary?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Not that I'm aware of, but I'm not an expert in antiphospholipid syndrome itself.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Did the antiphospholipid syndrome pass to either [Baby A] or to [Baby B]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, that is not the case. I can explain that in a little bit more detail because if one looked at the blood results, it would show that there were antiphospholipid antibodies in the circulation of the babies and this is because there are two types of antibody: IgM, immunoglobulin M, and IgA, immunoglobulin A -- sorry, IgG and IgM, sorry.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: I was going to say, I don't think we really need --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Obviously it's very helpful of you to offer to do it, but the important thing is that neither [Baby A] or [Baby B] had this condition.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That is correct, yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Right. I wasn't sure quite what was in issue and what wasn't.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Anyway, if you need -- you can explain how you can tell that, but it's basically from the blood that's taken? You'd find the antibodies in the blood?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You would find the antibodies in the blood, one type, only the IgG, which is not significant in the children.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We know, from the evidence that we heard, that the treating doctors at the time were concerned about this and were not sure that it hadn't passed, but you can say it didn't pass from mother to children?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, it didn't.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Thank you. You then at just before -- as part of your haematology results and interpretation section at the end of that section you deal with the question or the issue of air embolus.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And what remarks did you -- we'll come in more detail to air embolus in due course towards the end of your evidence, but what conclusions did you draw so far as air embolus was concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, the only conclusions that I was able to get was from the description of the doctors who attended [Baby A] and the features of the blotchiness on the skin, particularly the commentary about pallor and pinkness and blueness in the skin. And so I was quite brought up short, really, by hearing -reading about this and so that is -- that really cemented my concerns and the comments, particularly that Dr Jayaram had said about what was going on.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Did his description -- was his description consistent with a particular phenomenon?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Haemoglobin is a word that you've used on several occasions during your evidence. Assuming that we know nothing about it, can you explain what it is, please?

blocks.text: Yes. So haemoglobin, on this figure is the squiggly bit with the four bits that look like ping-pong balls in them. So this is a unit of haem. There are four groups of haem bound together and that is called haemoglobin, and each molecule of haemoglobin can bind oxygen.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: The haemoglobin is within the red blood cells and the red blood cells are sent round the body by the pumping action of the heart and the circulation. Just to explain, you'll see on the bottom right-hand side the deoxygenated bit, which is blue, without the white bit, which is the ping-pong ball, which is indicating haemoglobin -- sorry, the oxygen.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So haemoglobin without any oxygen is a blue colour.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: When you add oxygen to it by -- coming from the lungs, which we'll get on to, the haemoglobin changes to a red colour. So what's going to happen next is you're going to see features of slides where some of the blood is blue, that is low oxygenated blood, and some is red, which is oxygenated blood.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So it is haemoglobin's job within the red cells to transport oxygen around the body.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So that in effect is a pictorial representation of what you are explaining?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This is SK4.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. This is a picture of the tiniest parts of the lungs, which are called alveoli, one alveolus. This is where the lungs have developed tiny, tiny little pockets which are only one cell thick and at the same time the blood supply to that area is only one cell thick as well. So if you look on the lefthand side of the diagram here you'll see blue on the left-hand side, moving to pinker in the middle, and red to the right-hand side of that. So that is the tiniest blood vessel, called the arteriole, coming into contact with the small bit of the lung called the alveolus. It's obtaining the oxygen from the circulation, into the haemoglobin, making it turn pink, and then you can see that the pinkness becomes more, so that by the time we get to it right-hand side of the left-hand picture what's going out from the lungs is bright red.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The right-hand side is showing more clearly about the diffusion of the oxygen out of the alveolus. So if you take a deep breath in, there's more oxygen in the alveolus, and the red cells, as they are going back -- you see those little discs in the blood vessel running next to the alveolus -- and the oxygen moves across by diffusion. So the -- there's a gradient of high oxygen in the lungs and low in the blood vessels, so the oxygen diffuses through into the bluish looking red cells to pinken up the haemoglobin and it comes out in the capillary.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So does it come to this: the way these red cells are set up and the way the haemoglobin is set up is if it comes across oxygen, in effect it grabs the oxygen?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It does indeed, yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes, that's absolutely right.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And that's reflective of this exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the alveoli of the lungs?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it is, yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Can you tell us what an embolus is, first, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. So an embolus is something that shouldn't be there in the circulation. This does happen quite frequently in the
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: human population. So the most common time that we see an embolus is from a blood clot when some of the clot breaks off and then travels round in the circulation. So it's a loose body travelling around in the circulation. And you can see and understand from the way I've described to you that the vessels on the venous side of the circulation, that's the right side of the circulation, get narrower and narrower and narrower until they're oxygenated and those little capillaries get bigger and bigger and bigger. You can see there are times where the vessels get narrower and so the embolus gets stuck in the vessel, and it can't get through, the rest of the blood can't get through, and the oxygen within the blood cells can't get through either.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So anything beyond that stops flowing or, in fact, dies. So you may have heard of people who have had clots in their legs or in the pelvis, who have had a pulmonary embolus, to the lungs, and they've just dropped dead because that can happen. But that's a solid thing.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: It is possible to have other things that can be embolic. So it's possible to have a fat embolus with multiple trauma with many fractured bones, where bone marrow, which contains a lot of fat, gets into the circulation, so you can get fatty emboli.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And I think I have got something else in here as well. Yes. So the other time that emboli are slightly different -- but in narrowing of arteries, such as in the neck going up to the brain, you can have thrombi there, which can cause stroke, and you can get little bits of plaque coming from the coronary arteries so you get a heart attack. These are the things, the embolic things, that happen in the normal course of being a human being.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Very rarely you can get amniotic fluid embolus during childbirth where, by accident, amniotic fluid gets into the maternal circulation and that is usually fatal.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So an embolus is something that's in the wrong place. The important thing about it is it can get lodged and so it stops the circulation behind it, which is what does the damage.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: As it expands. So far as mechanisms go, that's quite a different mechanism from the exogenous introduction of air injected or that finds its way into the system of a baby, isn't it, by way of mechanism?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: By way of mechanism it is, but bubbles will enlarge and will be in the circulation already and therefore you then end up with emboli causing the bends, the pain that comes with that.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Again, the paper that we're dealing with focused on four adults, didn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It did, yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: It seems one relevant feature in that case was they were also four overweight adults, they had raised BMIs, didn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. There were many limitations to their findings.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And the reason I point that out is because their raised BMI is relevant because they had more subcutaneous fat and, from the paper, that affects the rate at which nitrogen might be released; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Again, this is decompression stuff that I'm not an expert in.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: All right. In any event, whilst that paper certainly goes to show the relationship between bubbles coming to the skin and decompression in those divers --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Who had patent --
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Yes, who did have. It is very specific to them in terms of the base of people that it's based upon, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it is, but also they did happen to have patent foramen ovale.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Yes. And was that paper the first paper dealing with reports of bubbles in the skin after diving as far as we can tell?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Again, I've said I'm not an expert in this area and I don't know the entire literature.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Do you agree that the paper, the research you have relied upon there, would be no basis for saying that bubbles in the blood would always cause a rash in deep sea divers?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I can't say that and I don't think that they can say that either.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: But that it always causes a rash, you can't say that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Could you repeat the question again?
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Just so we understand what you've relied upon, this paper, informing your opinion about bubbles and air embolus, it doesn't give a basis for saying, for instance, that bubbles in the blood will always cause a rash in divers who are suffering from decompression sickness, does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Right. And nor can it form a basis for saying that air introduced exogenously in a baby will always, for example, produce bubbles that will come to the skin and cause discolouration? It doesn't do that, does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it doesn't.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: I just want to move away from the research basis for what you've had to said to some more general questions about air in the blood as far as you can help us, Professor Kinsey.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We've seen from the material you've given us how tissues and blood will absorb oxygen when it's carried around the body.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: That's right, isn't it? And again, I repeat, that's illustrated by what was referred to as the ping-pong ball mechanism --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: -- the exchange of oxygen? I touched on this earlier: a large part of air is formed by nitrogen, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And what percentage did you say that was?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, it's about 71%.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: About 71%. All right. As we've established, nitrogen is not absorbed by the blood or body tissue in the way that oxygen is, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And it will remain in bubble form in the blood for very much longer, won't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I expect so.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And in fact, decompression sickness, when we're looking at that, can last for hours with divers, can't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: This isn't decompression.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: No, but one of the reasons it lasts for hours is because the nitrogen stays in the blood for quite a long time, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't know the answer to that, but I'm not sure we can compare it with decompression either because the amount of -the problem with decompression is the nitrogen is compressed and because it's a larger gas in air, as people come up to the surface the bubbles get larger.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: It's not the same because at sea level the bubbles are not going to change just because of nitrogen. So I don't think that is the right thing to say.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: You agree, you can't simply take what happens in decompression sickness and apply that to an air embolus?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, you can't.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Which again is one of the limitations with the paper you went to, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, it is. What I was -- I was explaining in using that was the fact that skin manifestations have been seen in deep sea divers on decompression who have patent foramen ovale.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: All right. If air is in the blood sufficient to cause a collapse, we're talking about air introduced exogenously, however that is, whether intentional or accidental, but air that's come in exogenously, that air will include the nitrogen and the oxygen, won't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: If it's caused a collapse, the nitrogen will still remain in the blood for some time even after the oxygen has been absorbed, won't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If the circulation has stopped then that is the case.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: But the oxygen -- the nitrogen is introduced by breathing.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Actually, that's not the case.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Nitrogen comes in exogenously, so it will stay around.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: It will, won't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So however it's entered the system, it will stay around.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And you've explained that the harm is done by blockages as the vessels get smaller?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: So if nitrogen is in the system, even if the oxygen is absorbed, the nitrogen will continue to block vessels for however long it takes for the nitrogen to stop?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And if that's the case, you wouldn't expect there to be what could be described as a rapid recovery if there was sufficient air to cause a collapse because of an air embolism, would you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It depends how big the embolism is.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: All right. But in principle, insofar as the blockage of vessels creates the harm, whatever that is, as long as there are nitrogen bubbles of sufficient size to create a blockage, that harm would continue?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, the harm really is in the size of the embolus and the size of the vessel it's in. So minuscule arterioles in the skin, it doesn't really matter if they get blocked up because there is a bypass circuit. But if you have a massive air bubble going into the arteries that lead to the brain then life will cease instantly.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Thank you for explaining that. But save for acknowledging that nitrogen takes much longer to be cleared from the system than oxygen, the continuing effect of it depends on how much there was that went in; is that what you'd say?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't think I would say -- I don't think I have an opinion on that because I don't know enough about it.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm not sure other people do either.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Thank you for dealing with that, Professor Kinsey. Would you give me one moment, please?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: (Pause)
Thank you for answering my questions.
Does your Lordship have any questions?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Questions from THE JUDGE
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just in relation to that very last answer that you gave, you won't give an opinion on that proposition that was put to you and you didn't think other people would have an opinion about it, if I understood your answer.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well...
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Can you just explain why you said that?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, my Lord. I have never encountered any discussion about nitrogen in the circulation except in deep sea divers. So the biggest effect of an air embolus would be the size of it, of course, and in the vessel that becomes blocked and what is beyond that vessel that then dies. Nobody has ever mentioned-in the cases I have needed to talk to people about air embolus, nobody's talked about the different quantities of the gases contained in air. So that's why I made the comment I did.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Right. 71% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, carbon dioxide?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And a few other things.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: And other smaller gases?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, inert gases.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, professor.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thank you very much, Professor Kinsey.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That completes your evidence at this stage. But you will be coming back, is that right, Mr Johnson?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You will be coming back at a future time to give evidence. Please do not discuss this case or anything to do with this case or your evidence and the areas of expertise about which you have given evidence with anyone else.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Just keep your thoughts to yourself until this case is all over, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: KINSEY

blocks.text: Thank you very much.

blocks.text: MR IAN ALLEN (affirmed)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
Could I invite you to begin by stating your full naming for the record, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: My name is Ian Christopher Allen.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: And your current occupation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm a regional quality assurance specialist pharmacist for the north-west of England.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: And your occupation in May 2015?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was the principal pharmacist for aseptic services at the Countess of Chester.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: And for how long did you undertake that role?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So from May 2015 to December 2019.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you tell us a little, please, about your academic qualifications that are relevant to that professional role that you undertook at the hospital?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, certainly. I have a master's degree in pharmacy.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: I have a postgraduate diploma in clinical pharmacy, and a postgraduate diploma in pharmaceutical technology and quality assurance.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you describe, in a sentence or two, the primary function of the aseptic unit at a hospital such as the Countess of Chester Hospital?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, certainly. The aseptic unit is a specialist area within the pharmacy for the preparation of injectable medicines. So the facility functions to ensure the quality and safety of the medicine that's prepared.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: During your time within that unit at that hospital, what was the nature of the intravenous bags produced within the unit for use within the neonatal department?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So we produce a range of products for the neonatal unit. One of them was intravenous feed, commonly referred to as TPN, total parenteral nutrition. We also provided a range of other injectable medicines, including antibiotics and other preprepared injections to be supplied to the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: We'll come back to those latter items in due course, but if we could, please, for the time being, focus upon the total parenteral nutrition bags that you and your department would have handled and ultimately provided to the neonatal unit about which this jury have already heard a little and indeed watched a video demonstration recording, which I believe, could you confirm, that you too had the benefit of seeing in the recent past?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. I have seen the video last week.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: Thank you. How many types of TPN bags did you come across during your time within the aseptic unit?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So prepared from the aseptic unit we would make Babiven Maintenance, which we would add vitamins and trace elements to. We also supplied out to the ward itself, but not made within the pharmacy aseptic unit, Babiven Start-up and Babiven Maintenance, but the one that was supplied to the ward directly would have no vitamins and trace elements inside it.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: So Babiven Start-up. We understand, could you confirm, if you agree, that that would be used for babies during the first day or two of life?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct, yes: for the first 2 days of life, the baby received Babiven Start-up.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: A second type of, if I might call it off-the-shelf TPN bag, you've already described as a Maintenance bag. And both of those, is this right, would be supplied to the unit through your department but without your department in any way adulterating the contents of the bag?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So Babiven Maintenance -- there would be Babiven Maintenance bags sent to stock, which we would not add anything to the bag. But also we would supply Babiven Maintenance with vitamins and trace elements.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: The difference being that it takes a little time to process an order from the pharmacy, so the ward might use the Babiven Maintenance without the vitamins and trace elements to start, but then once they had sent the order to the pharmacy, the baby would move on to have the bag with the vitamins and trace elements from that point forward.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's deal with the process by which an order for such a bag would be made by the NNU to the pharmacy department and the process by which it would be tailored to the specific requests and then supplied if you would.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Firstly, how would an initial order be received?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the order would be received via fax from the neonatal unit. So a prescription would be written on to a card by a doctor and that'd be faxed down to the pharmacy aseptic unit.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: Thank you. And upon receipt of that request, what would be the first stage in the process within the pharmacy unit?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that would be handed to a pharmacist, such as myself.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: The pharmacist would review the prescription, to ensure it's prescribed correctly against the standard protocol.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: The pharmacist would then process that prescription into a worksheet, which is essentially an instruction for how to make the TPN bag.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: So a clinician would effectively send a prescription, the content of that prescription would be transformed into a
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: worksheet, which is a set of instructions, effectively; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct, yes. The worksheet itself would be instructions on how to make the bag but also a list of the ingredients which are used to prepare the bag, so a list of what would need to be gathered to make it.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: So you have the menu and the instructions on how to introduce those ingredients into the bag and in what proportions?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: Next please. Might I ask you about the next step in the manufacturing process?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, certainly. So from that point forward, after the worksheet -- and a label would be generated at the same time for the bag -- the next step would be for a member of the pharmacy team, either a pharmacy assistant or technician, to gather the ingredients used to make the bag. So on the worksheet is a list of exactly what materials are needed and the quantities. They would gather from the shelves in the pharmacy those specific materials and quantities.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: So it would be a bag of Babiven Maintenance, a vial of water, a vial of -- an ampoule of water, sorry, a vial of Solivito, and an ampoule of Peditrace. So they would gather those ingredients and then copy down the batch numbers from those ingredients -so every medicine comes with a pre-printed batch number which is specific to it. They would be written down on to the work sheet to record what been used to make the bag. So we would call that process assembly because you're gathering together ingredients.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: And this assembly element of the process, would that be done in a creative way or would it be done by way of adherence to strict and well-established protocols?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So every step in the whole process of making the bag has a -- what's called a standard operating procedure, so a standard step-by-step process, which staff have to follow. The idea is that that makes the process repeatable and of a high quality level. Staff would have to sign to read those procedures and they would be trained in how to follow them.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but you do speak very quickly. I'm conscious that someone who is transcribing what you're saying, even a speed writer, will have difficulty with keeping up with you. Could you just slow down a bit, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No problem, yes.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: You speak quickly naturally. I'm not being critical, but for the benefit of other people.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'll slow down.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: Mr Allen, I think the answer you just provided to me is a description of -- is it appropriate to describe it as a quality assurance protocol?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, so that would be correct: it's a quality assured process. There are regulatory standards which have to be followed in terms of how we produce the bag, nationally recognised regulatory standards.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: So those standards are set by a regulatory body outwith the hospital?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct. So the part of EU law is called Good Manufacturing Practice which defines the standards for preparation of a medicine.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: And were those standards adopted and embraced within the pharmacy unit whilst you worked there?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct, yes, they were.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: You described to us the process by which specifically prescribed elements might be gathered together and added to a manufactured bag that had been bought into the hospital. After that is done, what is the next step of the process?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So after the ingredients have been checked, they would then be passed into the aseptic clean rooms. So this is a specially designed room which has clean air blown into it through special filters, so it's controlling all the air in that environment.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: What we would do is we would spray the exterior of those items with 70% alcohol. The idea is that kills any microorganisms which are present on the exterior of those items as they're transferred into this controlled environment.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: So there's two steps of this, where they are sprayed and wiped with alcohol and a sporicidal. And through this process they make their way to a clean-air device, which we refer to as a laminar airflow cabinet. This is the place where the actual manipulations are going to take place.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: So the rooms themselves have controlled air, then the cabinet or the laminar airflow cabinet has controlled clean air blown into it. It's all about reducing the amount of micro-organisms in the environment where the bag is going to be made.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: All designed to ensure the sterility of the process and thereby the sterility of the product?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: The bags, having been tailored to match the prescription, details of which had been transformed into a worksheet of instructions, I should say, what happens next?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So inside the clean air device, which was demonstrated on the video itself, there will be two operators who will actually make the bag. What they are going to do is take materials from the ampoules and vials which have been assembled. They will add from -- one of those ampoules gets pulled up and added directly to the bag.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: Another of the manipulations is to take some water and add to that to a vial -- we call that staff(?) reconstitution because it has got a powder inside and you are adding water to the powder. That is then pulled up and added to the bag itself.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: There's a series of checks in place so we always work with two operators who are confirming both the identity of the ingredients against the worksheet, but also the volume that has been withdrawn and added to the bag.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: After that takes place, the bag will be mixed.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: So you've just described to us in detail how the bag or its content, more accurately, are prepared and the environment within which those preparations take place.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And is it still within that same sterile environment that a second employee checks all that has just gone on before?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct. So just to be clear, there's a check whilst the bag has been made, so there's always two operators who are making the bag. But then there's another check once it's passed out of that cabinet as well by an independent -- what we call a releasing pharmacist will check.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: So the two pharmacy assistants or operatives work together and check each other's conduct --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: -- professional conduct? And we saw from the video, and we'll watch it again in a moment, does the bag pass through a controlled out-hatch --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: -- into a different room or part of a room, and on the other side of there, does a pharmacist undertake something akin to a defect check?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. That is the releasing process where the pharmacist is checking all aspects of the preparation and the worksheet. They also perform what's called reconciliation, where they take the used ampoules and vials and they check what's used, they check that back against the worksheet to make sure the correct items have been used during the actual preparation of the bag.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: And how would that checking pharmacist satisfy him or herself that the correct items have been used?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So they would have access to the prescription to understand what had been prescribed, so they check against that. So they check the worksheet back against the prescription itself.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: They then take each ampoule or vial, which would now be empty, which had been passed out, they would again check those against the list of ingredients on that worksheet and sign for that check.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: Who is ultimately responsible?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The releasing pharmacist would be ultimately responsible for the product.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: You made mention of a regulatory regime which dictates the process that you have us just described to us. Is the unit itself subject to regulatory monitoring?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It is. So the unit had -- operated under two regulatory frameworks. Under one of them it prepared items under section 10 of the Medicines Act. And that was a requirement from the HS that there would be inspections via a regional quality assurance auditor.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: The unit also held a MHRA manufacturer's specials licence and was subject to inspection by the MHRA.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: Forgive me if this is an invitation for you to state the obvious, but what is the underlying purpose of these regulatory
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: protocols and this systematic approach to the production of these bags?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It is to ensure the quality, safety and efficacy of the medicine, to make sure that what is prescribed, the product that we actually make, meets the patient's needs and is both safe and effective and of the required level of quality.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, we are simply kind of an intermediary: we receive them from the manufacturer, we have a big fridge to store them in, the bulk of the stock. Then we send them up in small amounts to the smaller fridge in the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: My Lord, if I may assist, Nurse Yvonne Griffiths will give evidence tomorrow --
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I didn't know whether we were --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: -- on this topic and she'll produce, as an exhibit, the requisition sheets sent from the neonatal unit to the pharmacy unit for the relevant period.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Right, she will deal with the other matter then about what happens to the bags afterwards and any unused bags and things like that. All right, good.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I don't have any more questions. Thank you very much, Mr Allen — that will be it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's Mr Allen's only visit to the witness box.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Good. Thank you very much for coming and giving your evidence this afternoon. That completes your evidence. You are free to go.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Should it be that you encounter anyone who is involved in this case, don't talk about anything to do with the case until it's all over.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ALLEN

blocks.text: Thank you very much indeed, Mr Allen.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)

All right, members of the jury, that's it for today. Can I just say this: we have heard quite a lot of evidence today of an expert nature and indeed the witness herself, the professor, referred to the fact that she gleaned some of the material, namely those diagrams that she produced, from the internet, which raises the obvious point that it is very possible to gain information from the internet.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So I repeat what I have said to you many times before: do not conduct any research into anything to do with this case, so don't start going on to the internet to try and find these diagrams for yourselves. All right? If there is anything upon which you require further exposition, you can ask a question about it, but don't conduct any of your personal research. Whilst I'm saying that, I remind you of the other vital obligation of you as jurors not to speak to anyone about anything to do with this case or each other unless you are all together in the room outside this court. All right?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Please remember those obligations. But that's a timely opportunity to remind you of them because you've had a specific example of what can be gained on the internet and there's an awful lot more, as we know. I shall keep reminding you of that during the case. Thank you very much indeed.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: 10.30 tomorrow morning then. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The court adjourned until 10.30 am on Wednesday, 30 November 2022)
